scripts.hook: One scene in Groundhog Day explains how people actually change.
scripts.hook_b: Phil Connors lives the same day over and over. Watch what he does.
cards: One scene in Groundhog Day explains how people actually change.
Phil Connors relives the same day. Over and over.
First he uses it for himself. It works. It's empty.

Same boy.
Same tree.
Every day.
He catches him every time. The boy never says thanks.
Aristotle said it 2,300 years earlier: you become brave by doing brave things.
Idea: Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (Ross) · Moodius words
You become what you rehearse. That's how people change.

source.author: Aristotle
source.verified_at: plan.md section 4 ✓ (25 Oct); Ross 1908 public domain

scripts.caption:
Groundhog Day (1993, dir. Harold Ramis) is a comedy about the oldest idea in ethics. Phil only changes once he stops using the repeated day for himself and starts using it for other people: lessons, small rescues, a boy who never says thanks.

Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (tr. W. D. Ross): “we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”

Your ordinary day repeats too. Send this to the friend who’s been having the same Tuesday since March.

Film analysis by Moodius. No footage used.

Your same day?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: Your watch says 10,000 steps or you failed.
scripts.hook_b: How many steps a day does the research actually support?
cards: Your watch says 10,000 steps or you failed.

2022 · 15 STUDIES
About 47,000 adults, followed for years.
Where did the benefit level off?

6,000–8,000 a day if you're over 60.
8,000–10,000 if you're under.
2025, 57 studies: about 7,000 a day gave most of the benefit linked to 10,000.
Paluch et al., 2022 · Ding et al., 2025 · Lancet Public Health
More steps than you do now still counts.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Labelled cards carry the Ember label line (study, then evidence).

source.author: Paluch et al.; Ding et al.
source.section: daily steps and all-cause mortality: benefit rises then levels off; ~7,000 steps gives most of the benefit linked to 10,000

scripts.caption:
10,000 steps is a round number, not a finish line. A 2022 meta-analysis of 15 cohorts (about 47,000 adults) found the drop in risk of death levelled off around 6,000–8,000 steps a day for adults over 60 and 8,000–10,000 for younger adults. A 2025 review of 57 studies found about 7,000 steps a day was linked to a 47% lower risk of death than 2,000, close to the figure for 10,000.

These are observational studies: they show links, not proof that steps cause the benefit. If you're at 3,000, 5,000 is progress.

Send this to the friend whose watch has been nagging them since January.

Sources: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health 7(3), 2022 · Ding et al., Lancet Public Health, 2025. General information, not medical advice.

Your number?

— Moodius

scripts.hook: A cook explained effortless work to his ruler.
scripts.hook_b: The secret of effortless work, from a cook, 2,300 years ago.
cards: A cook explained effortless work to his ruler.
China, 2,300 years ago. The cook is carving an ox.
The ruler asks: how did your skill get so perfect?

Not strength.
Not a sharper knife.
Nineteen years.
“Now my knife has been in use for nineteen years”
Zhuangzi, Book III · tr. James Legge, 1891
He learned where the gaps are. The blade goes through the spaces.
Effortless is what nineteen years of work looks like.
What's your Cook Ding skill? Answer below.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, type only. Quote card in Playfair italic.

source.author: Zhuangzi
source.section: Book III, Nourishing the Lord of Life
source.translation: James Legge (Sacred Books of the East XXXIX, 1891)

scripts.caption:
In the Zhuangzi, a cook carves an ox for his ruler so smoothly it sounds like music. Asked how, he says his knife has been in use for nineteen years and is still sharp, because he follows the spaces between the joints instead of hacking at the bone. The ruler replies that he has just learned how to nourish his life.

The skill that looks like ease is usually nineteen years of paying attention. (Moodius's reading of Zhuangzi, Book III, tr. James Legge.)

Send this to the friend who makes a hard thing look easy.

— Moodius

scripts.hook_b: Psychologists found a gap in almost every first conversation.
cards: They probably liked you more than you think.
Afterwards, who did they rate higher: themselves or their partner?

Their partner.
Most people underestimated how much they were liked.
With real roommates, the gap lasted for months.
The liking gap · Boothby et al., Psychological Science, 2018
You're grading your awkward bits. They're enjoying the talk.
Send the follow-up text. The conversation went better than you think.
Send this to the friend who replays conversations.

source.author: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark
source.work: The liking gap in conversations (Psychological Science, 2018)
source.section: people underestimate how much conversation partners like them; lasted months among roommates

scripts.caption:
After a conversation with someone new, most of us think it went worse than it did. Psychologists call it the liking gap: in five-minute chats between strangers, people consistently underestimated how much the other person liked them. A study of college roommates found the gap lasted for months.

It's an average, not a promise. But it means the text you're not sending is probably more welcome than you think.

Send this to the friend who replays conversations at 2am.

Source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark, Psychological Science (2018).

Who'd you text?

— Moodius
